title: Costco Stock Price: What’s Driving the Recent Rally?
summary: Find out why Costco stock price is climbing, its year‑to‑date gain, latest price near May record, October sales, and high P/E ratio.
intro: Costco shares have surged this year, climbing about 20% after six straight earnings beats. As of November 2026 the stock is hovering near its May record high of $1,094, fueled by strong October sales and solid comparable growth. Investors are watching the rally closely, weighing the impressive earnings against a lofty trailing P/E of 49x.
bullets: Six consecutive earnings beats
Stock up ~20% YTD
Near $1,094 May record high
October net sales $24.5 billion
Trailing P/E at 49x

sections.heading: What has driven Costco's recent stock price rally?
sections.text: Costco’s rally is rooted in a streak of earnings surprises. Six straight beats have lifted the share price about 20% this year, according to a 247wallst.com report dated November 6, 2026. The company’s October net sales rose 12.6% year over year to $24.5 billion, reinforcing the earnings narrative. Analysts also highlighted comparable sales growth—11.1% overall and 7.3% when gas and currency effects are stripped out—signaling robust consumer demand across the warehouse chain.

sections.heading: How much has Costco stock increased so far this year?
sections.text: As of early November 2026, Costco shares have risen roughly 20% year‑to‑date. The 247wallst.com article notes six consecutive earnings beats contributed to this gain. CNBC reported that the stock had climbed more than 19% since bottoming out in mid‑September, confirming a strong upward trajectory within a short period.

sections.heading: What is Costco's current price relative to its May record high?
sections.text:
On Thursday, November 5, 2026, Costco Wholesale Corp. (NASDAQ: COST) rallied close to 2 percent, nudging the share price to just under its May record high of $1,094. That level, first set in early May, now sits only a few dollars away from the current market price, underscoring the strength of the momentum that has carried the stock higher over the past several months.

The climb is anchored in a string of six consecutive earnings beats, which have propelled Costco’s shares up roughly 20 percent year‑to‑date, according to a 247WallSt.com report published on November 6. Since bottoming out in mid‑September, the stock has surged more than 19 percent, a rebound driven by robust top‑line growth and resilient consumer demand. In October alone, Costco reported net sales of $24.5 billion—a 12.6 percent increase versus the same month a year earlier—and comparable sales rose 11.1 percent year over year. When gas sales and currency effects are stripped out, comparable sales still climbed 7.3 percent, a figure highlighted by Goldman Sachs analysts in the CNBC coverage of the earnings release.

While the price action is impressive, the valuation remains demanding. Costco’s trailing price‑to‑earnings multiple sits at about 49 times earnings, reflecting investors’ willingness to pay a premium for the retailer’s consistent performance and strong membership base. Nonetheless, the proximity to the $1,094 peak signals that the market still believes the company’s growth trajectory can justify such lofty multiples, at least in the near term.

intro: The Woodlands, TX offers a high‑income, well‑educated community with extensive green space, major corporate campuses, and easy access to Houston. While housing and rent are pricey, the area’s amenities and quality of life rank it among the most sought‑after suburbs in the Greater Houston region.

sections.heading: Population and Demographics
sections.text:
The Woodlands is a fast‑growing special‑purpose district and census‑designated place that straddles Montgomery and Harris counties, just 28 miles north of downtown Houston along I‑45.  According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2020‑2024 American Community Survey, the community’s population stands at roughly 121,000 residents, up from 114,436 recorded in the 2020 decennial census.  The median age of 40.6 years points to a balanced mix of families, established professionals, and retirees, while the per‑capita income of $67,290 and median household income of $140,701 signal a relatively affluent populace.

Housing data reinforce the picture of stability: about 73 % of occupied units are owner‑occupied, with a median home value of $511,700.  Renters face a median gross rent of $1,822 per month, reflecting the area’s desirability and limited rental inventory.  Spread across 43.9 square miles—43.3 square miles of land and only 0.58 square miles of water—the community enjoys a low‑density, forest‑rich environment that feels far removed from the high‑rise bustle of central Houston.  The Woodlands Township, governed by an elected board of directors, oversees this sprawling suburb, which forms part of the larger Woodlands‑Conroe urban area of 402,454 people, ranking it the 103rd‑largest urban area in the United States.  These demographic and geographic factors combine to create a stable, well‑earned reputation as a premium place to live within the Greater Houston region.

sections.heading: Economy and Major Employers
sections.text:
The Woodlands is a hub for energy and healthcare firms. Major corporations with campuses include Occidental Petroleum Corporation, Chevron Phillips Chemical, Huntsman Corporation, Woodforest National Bank, Baker Hughes, McKesson Specialty Health, and Halliburton. These employers contribute to a median household income of $140,701 and a per‑capita income of $67,290, positioning the community well above national averages. The presence of these firms also supports a robust local service sector.

The Woodlands Township, governed by an elected board, manages community services and infrastructure, reinforcing the area's reputation for well‑planned development.

The higher price tags are offset for many residents by a robust median household income of $140,701—well above the U.S. median. This strong earning power gives a large portion of the population the ability to purchase or lease comfortably, contributing to the area’s 73 % owner‑occupancy rate. Homebuyers benefit from long‑term stability, as the majority of households tend to stay put, fostering tight‑knit neighborhoods and well‑maintained properties.

However, the cost barrier is real for lower‑income families and newcomers without the benefit of high salaries. Renters paying close to $2,000 a month must allocate a sizable share of their income to housing, which can limit discretionary spending on other necessities. Prospective residents should weigh the trade‑off between The Woodlands’ desirable lifestyle—forested streets, a humid subtropical climate, and easy access to Houston via I‑45—and the premium required to live there.

sections.text: The Woodlands is heavily forested, with terrain ranging from 125 to 175 feet above sea level, offering natural scenery throughout the 43.9‑square‑mile area. title: The Woodlands vs Cedar Park: Which Is Right for You?
summary: Compare size, income, rent, home values and lifestyle of The Woodlands and Cedar Park to decide where to live.
intro: The Woodlands and Cedar Park are two fast‑growing Texas communities that often appear on home‑search lists. The Woodlands is larger, richer and more owner‑focused, while Cedar Park offers a slightly younger population and comparable housing costs. This guide breaks down the hard data so you can see which community matches your priorities.
bullets: The Woodlands has 55% more residents than Cedar Park.
Median household income is $11,156 higher in The Woodlands.
Rent is about 1% lower in The Woodlands.
Home values are nearly identical in both markets.

sections.heading: Population size and density
sections.text: The Woodlands is home to 121,002 people, while Cedar Park’s population stands at 78,301. That makes The Woodlands about 42,701 residents larger, or roughly 55% more people than Cedar Park. The Woodlands spreads across 43.9 square miles, giving it a lower overall density than Cedar Park, which is smaller in both land area and headcount. A larger population can mean more amenities, diverse dining options and a broader commuter base, while a smaller community often feels tighter‑knit and easier to navigate.

sections.heading: Income levels and purchasing power
sections.text:
Median household income in The Woodlands is $140,701 per year, compared with $129,545 in Cedar Park—a difference of $11,156, or roughly a 9 % advantage for The Woodlands. This income gap is reflected in the broader economic picture of each community. With a population of 121,002, The Woodlands supports a larger tax base than Cedar Park’s 78,301 residents, allowing the township‑run municipal services to fund extensive amenities such as well‑maintained parks, a robust public‑safety department, and a variety of cultural programs. The higher average earnings also translate into greater discretionary spending; residents can more comfortably afford dining, entertainment, and boutique shopping, which in turn sustains a vibrant local economy.

Cedar Park, while earning a respectable median income, shows a slightly higher rent burden—median gross rent of $1,846 versus $1,822 in The Woodlands. When expressed as a share of household income, rent consumes about 17 % of a Cedar Park household’s earnings, compared with roughly 16 % in The Woodlands. This modest difference suggests that The Woodlands’ residents enjoy a marginally larger financial cushion for savings or lifestyle choices. Home‑ownership rates further illustrate purchasing power: 73 % of occupied units in The Woodlands are owner‑occupied versus 67 % in Cedar Park, indicating a stronger capacity to invest in real‑estate assets. Together, these figures imply that The Woodlands is likely to attract high‑earning professionals and families seeking both higher income potential and the financial flexibility to leverage that earnings into property, leisure, and community involvement.

sections.heading: Rent costs and affordability ratios
sections.text: The median gross rent in The Woodlands is $1,822 per month, just $24 less than Cedar Park’s $1,846. When measured against household income, rent in The Woodlands equals about 16% of the median income, while Cedar Park’s rent equals about 17%. Both cities keep rent below the conventional 30% affordability threshold, but The Woodlands offers a marginally lower rent‑to‑income ratio, making it slightly more affordable for renters relative to earnings.

sections.heading: Home values and ownership rates
sections.text: Owner‑occupied homes in The Woodlands have a median value of $511,700, while Cedar Park’s median sits at $513,600—a $1,900 difference that is essentially negligible. About 73% of occupied housing units in The Woodlands are owner‑occupied, compared with 67% in Cedar Park. The higher ownership rate suggests a more stable, long‑term resident base in The Woodlands, whereas Cedar Park has a modestly larger share of renters.

sections.heading: What each community is known for
sections.text: The Woodlands is a special‑purpose district within the Greater Houston metro area, known for its master‑planned neighborhoods, extensive park system and township‑style governance. Its proximity to Houston (28 miles north) offers easy access to a major international airport and corporate headquarters. Cedar Park, part of the Austin‑Round Rock metropolitan region, is recognized for its family‑friendly atmosphere and relatively younger median age of 37.7 years. Both locations benefit from humid subtropical climates, but The Woodlands experiences slightly cooler winter highs of 60 °F compared with Cedar Park’s similar climate.

sections.heading: Who each city suits best
sections.text: If you value a larger community, higher household income, a higher home‑ownership rate and a slightly lower rent burden, The Woodlands aligns well with professionals, affluent families and retirees seeking a suburban feel with easy Houston access. Cedar Park appeals to younger families, first‑time homebuyers and those who prefer a tighter community with comparable housing costs and a modestly younger demographic. Both cities provide strong economic fundamentals; the choice hinges on lifestyle preferences, commute patterns and the importance of community size.

title: Is Cedar Park, TX a Good Place to Live? Pros and Cons
summary: Explore Cedar Park, TX’s demographics, housing, commute, amenities and history to decide if it’s right for you.
intro: Cedar Park, TX offers a high median household income of $129,545, a growing population of about 79,032, and easy access to Austin. With a median home value of $513,600 and a median rent of $1,846, the city balances suburban comfort with urban proximity. Below are the main advantages and drawbacks to help you determine if Cedar Park is a good place to live.
bullets: Median income $129,545
Home value $513,600
16 miles to downtown Austin
67% owner‑occupied housing
Rich prehistoric and frontier history

sections.heading: Population, Age and Income Profile
sections.text: The 2020‑2024 ACS estimates put Cedar Park’s population at 78,301, with the 2025 estimate at 79,032. Residents have a median age of 37.7 years, indicating a mix of families and professionals. A median household income of $129,545 places the city well above the national average, supporting a comfortable standard of living. About 67% of occupied housing units are owner‑occupied, reflecting a stable, invested community.

sections.heading: Location, Commute and Major Highways
sections.text: Cedar Park sits roughly 16 miles (26 km) northwest of downtown Austin, making daily commutes feasible for those working in the capital. U.S. Route 183 runs north‑south through the city, while the 183A Toll Road bypass, opened on March 15, 2007, eases east‑west traffic. Additional east‑west routes include RM‑1431/Whitestone Boulevard and Cypress Creek/Brushy Creek Road, providing multiple options for reaching Austin and surrounding areas.

sections.heading: Housing Costs and Ownership
sections.text: The median gross rent in Cedar Park is $1,846 per month, while the median value of owner‑occupied homes stands at $513,600. With roughly 67 % of the 25.6‑square‑mile city’s housing units owner‑occupied, the market leans toward long‑term residency rather than short‑term rentals. Cedar Park’s median household income of $129,545—well above the national average—helps offset the higher home prices, making homeownership attainable for many families, especially those drawn by the city’s strong schools and proximity to Austin’s tech corridor. For renters, the $1,846 rent figure is comparable to other Austin suburbs such as Round Rock and Pflugerville, yet it reflects the desirability of a community that offers newer subdivisions, easy access to U.S. Route 183 and the 183A toll road, and a relatively young median age of 37.7 years. Prospective buyers should weigh the $513,600 median home value against the city’s robust income levels and the fact that most residents stay put, which can translate into stable neighborhood cohesion and property appreciation. Meanwhile, renters benefit from a well‑maintained rental stock and the option to live within a city that blends suburban comfort with quick commutes—just 16 miles northwest of downtown Austin—while still enjoying amenities like the H‑E‑B Center and abundant green space.

sections.heading: Local Amenities and Entertainment
sections.text:
Cedar Park’s entertainment hub is the H‑E‑B Center at Cedar Park, a 5,000‑seat multipurpose indoor arena that opened in 2009. The venue draws national touring acts, minor‑league hockey (the Texas Stars), and a rotating slate of community events such as high‑school graduations, craft fairs, and charity runs, giving residents cultural and recreational options without a daily commute to Austin. Because the arena sits just off U.S. Route 183, it’s easily reachable from the city’s main north‑south corridor and from the 183A Toll Road, which cuts travel time to downtown Austin to under 30 minutes.

Shopping and dining are concentrated along the bustling Whitestone Boulevard (RM‑1431) and Cypress Creek/Brushy Creek Road corridors, where you’ll find national retailers, boutique stores, and a growing farm‑to‑table restaurant scene that reflects the city’s median household income of $129,545 and its relatively young median age of 37.7 years. Outdoor enthusiasts benefit from more than 30  miles of interconnected trails—including the Brushy Creek Regional Trail—that weave through the city’s 25.6 square‑mile footprint, linking neighborhoods to parks such as Cedar Park Center and the historic Wilson‑Leonard archaeological site.

Housing reflects the area’s prosperity: about 67 % of occupied units are owner‑occupied, with a median home value of $513,600, while renters face a median gross rent of $1,846 per month. This mix of modern amenities, easy highway access, and plentiful green space makes Cedar Park a well‑rounded suburb for families, young professionals, and retirees alike.

sections.heading: Historical Roots and Community Identity
sections.text: Long before European settlement, the area was home to the Tonkawa, Lipan Apache and Comanche tribes. Archaeological work at the Wilson‑Leonard site shows continuous habitation since circa 5,000 BC. In the mid‑19th century the community was known as Running Brushy, named for a spring that fed a local creek. George and Harriet Cluck’s 1873 purchase of 329 acres anchored the town’s development, and the arrival of the Austin and Northwestern Railroad about a decade later linked Cedar Park to larger markets, shaping its growth into the modern suburb it is today.

faq.a: The 2020‑2024 ACS estimates list Cedar Park’s population at 78,301, and the 2025 estimate is 79,032.

faq.a: Cedar Park lies about 16 miles (26 km) northwest of downtown Austin, making a typical commute under 30 minutes depending on traffic.

faq.a: U.S. Route 183 runs north‑south, the 183A Toll Road bypass opened March 15, 2007, and east‑west routes include RM‑1431/Whitestone Boulevard and Cypress Creek/Brushy Creek Road.

faq.q: What entertainment venues are located in Cedar Park?
faq.a: The H‑E‑B Center at Cedar Park, completed in 2009, is the city’s primary indoor arena for concerts, sports and community events.

For renters, the $1,846 rent figure is comparable to other Austin suburbs such as Round Rock and Pflugerville, yet it reflects the desirability of a community that offers newer subdivisions, easy access to U.S. Route 183 and the 183A toll road, and a relatively young median age of 37.7 years. Prospective buyers should weigh the $513,600 median home value against the city’s robust income levels and the fact that most residents stay put, which can translate into stable neighborhood cohesion and property appreciation. Meanwhile, renters benefit from a well‑maintained rental stock and the option to live within a city that blends suburban comfort with quick commutes—just 16 miles northwest of downtown Austin—while still enjoying amenities like the H‑E‑B Center and abundant green space.

Cedar Park’s entertainment hub is the H‑E‑B Center at Cedar Park, a 5,000‑seat multipurpose indoor arena that opened in 2009. The venue draws national touring acts, minor‑league hockey (the Texas Stars), and a rotating slate of community events such as high‑school graduations, craft fairs, and charity runs, giving residents cultural and recreational options without a daily commute to Austin. Because the arena sits just off U.S. Route 183, it’s easily reachable from the city’s main north‑south corridor and from the 183A Toll Road, which cuts travel time to downtown Austin to under 30 minutes.

Shopping and dining are concentrated along the bustling Whitestone Boulevard (RM‑1431) and Cypress Creek/Brushy Creek Road corridors, where you’ll find national retailers, boutique stores, and a growing farm‑to‑table restaurant scene that reflects the city’s median household income of $129,545 and its relatively young median age of 37.7 years. Housing reflects the area’s prosperity: about 67 % of occupied units are owner‑occupied, with a median home value of $513,600, while renters face a median gross rent of $1,846 per month. This mix of modern amenities, easy highway access, and plentiful green space makes Cedar Park a well‑rounded suburb for families, young professionals, and retirees alike.

Long before European settlement, the area was home to the Tonkawa, Lipan Apache and Comanche tribes. Archaeological work at the Wilson‑Leonard site shows continuous habitation since circa 5,000 BC. George and Harriet Cluck’s 1873 purchase of 329 acres anchored the town’s development, and the arrival of the Austin and Northwestern Railroad about a decade later linked Cedar Park to larger markets, shaping its growth into the modern suburb it is today.

Cedar Park combines strong earnings, a stable housing market and convenient access to Austin, while offering its own cultural venues and a deep historical backdrop. Weigh the higher home values against the income levels and commute distance to decide if the suburb fits your lifestyle.

title: The Woodlands vs Arlington: Which Is Right for You?
summary: Compare The Woodlands and Arlington on size, income, rent, home values, affordability and lifestyle to decide where to move.
intro: The Woodlands and Arlington differ sharply in population, earnings, housing costs and overall vibe. The Woodlands boasts higher incomes and home values but a smaller community, while Arlington offers more affordable rent and a larger, younger population. This guide breaks down the numbers and who each city serves best.

Home values: $511,700 in The Woodlands, $304,700 in Arlington.

sections.heading: Population and Size
sections.text: The Woodlands is a special‑purpose district covering 43.9 square miles with a 2020‑2024 ACS population of 121,002. Arlington is a much larger city, housing 397,742 people—about 276,740 more, or roughly 229% higher than The Woodlands. Arlington’s larger population translates into a denser urban feel and more varied neighborhoods, while The Woodlands feels more like a spacious, planned community surrounded by forested land.

sections.heading: Income Levels and Economic Profile
sections.text:
Median household income in The Woodlands is $140,701, which is $65,530—about 87 % higher than Arlington’s median of $75,171.  This disparity reflects the Woodlands’ concentration of professional, managerial, and executive households, many of whom work in energy, healthcare, and technology firms that dominate the Greater Houston economy.  The higher earnings translate into greater discretionary spending power; for example, the median gross rent in the Woodlands is $1,822 per month, roughly 16 % of its median income, compared with Arlington’s $1,470 rent, which consumes about 23 % of a typical household’s earnings. The economic profile is further shaped by demographics.  The Woodlands’ median age is 40.6 years, indicating a more established, higher‑earning population, whereas Arlington’s median age is 33.7 years, reflecting a younger, often earlier‑career cohort.  Despite its smaller size—121,002 residents versus Arlington’s 397,742—the Woodlands commands a premium market that supports upscale retail, fine‑dining, and extensive recreational amenities.  Prospective residents who prioritize higher income potential, greater home‑ownership rates, and the ability to allocate a larger share of earnings toward lifestyle choices may find The Woodlands a better fit, while those comfortable with a more modest income landscape and a younger community might lean toward Arlington.

sections.heading: Rent Costs and Affordability
sections.text: The median gross rent in The Woodlands is $1,822 per month, $352—or about 24%—higher than Arlington’s $1,470. Although The Woodlands rent is higher, it represents a smaller slice of earnings, making it relatively affordable for its residents, while Arlington renters face a larger income burden.

sections.text: Owner‑occupied homes in The Woodlands command a median value of $511,700, which is $207,000—about 68 % higher—than Arlington’s median of $304,700. The community’s wealthier profile is also evident in rental costs—median gross rent in The Woodlands is $1,822 per month, roughly 24 % more than Arlington’s $1,470. Yet rent consumes a smaller slice of income in The Woodlands (about 16 % of median household earnings) than in Arlington (about 23 %). These figures paint The Woodlands as a more affluent, settled market where homeownership is the norm and properties carry a premium price tag. Arlington, by contrast, offers a more accessible entry point for first‑time buyers and renters, with lower home values, a younger median age (33.7 vs. 40.6 years), and a higher proportion of renters. Your choice between the two will hinge on whether you prioritize a higher‑value, ownership‑heavy environment or a more budget‑friendly, entry‑level market.

sections.heading: What Each City Is Known For
sections.text: The Woodlands is recognized for its heavily forested landscape, extensive municipal services provided by the Woodlands Township, and its proximity—28 miles north—to Houston. Its design emphasizes green spaces and a suburban feel within the Greater Houston metro area. Arlington, part of the Dallas‑Fort Worth region, is known for its larger urban footprint, younger median age of 33.7 years, and a mix of residential, commercial, and entertainment districts that cater to a diverse, active population.

sections.heading: Who Should Choose Which City
sections.text: If you prioritize higher earnings, larger homes, and a family‑oriented, tree‑lined environment, The Woodlands suits professionals and families seeking stability and space. Its higher ownership rate and lower rent‑to‑income ratio appeal to those looking to invest in property. Arlington fits younger adults, first‑time renters, or buyers who want a more affordable market and a bustling city atmosphere. The larger population provides more nightlife, dining and cultural options, making it attractive for those who thrive in a livelier setting.

faq.a: The Woodlands median rent is $1,822 per month, about $352 higher than Arlington’s $1,470.

faq.q: Which is better for families, The Woodlands or Arlington?
faq.a: The Woodlands, with a higher homeownership rate (73%), larger median home value and a more suburban, forested setting, generally aligns better with family needs for space and stability.

faq.a: Arlington is larger, with a population of 397,742 compared with The Woodlands’ 121,002.

title: Is Scottsdale, AZ a Good Place to Live? Pros and Cons
summary: Explore Scottsdale, AZ's population, housing costs, climate, economy and lifestyle to decide if it's a good place to live.
intro: Scottsdale, AZ scores high on income and amenities, but its hot summers and pricey housing can be challenging. With a population of about 243,821, a median household income of $110,886 and a median home value near $789,800, the city offers comfort for many, yet cost considerations remain. Below we weigh the key pros and cons to help you decide if Scottsdale fits your lifestyle.
bullets: High median income and strong tourism economy
Housing costs above national average
Arid climate with extreme summer heat
Rapid growth and extensive outdoor recreation

sections.heading: Population Size and Growth Trends
sections.text:
Scottsdale’s 2020-2024 American Community Survey estimates the city’s population at 243,821, up from 241,361 in the 2020 census and 217,385 in 2010. The city’s growth reflects its status as one of the fastest‑expanding housing markets in the United States over the past two decades. Residents tend to be older, with a median age of 49 years, which influences the community’s pace and services. The city’s incorporation in 1951 began with just 2,000 people, showing how dramatically it has expanded.

These numbers signal a stable, mature community, but also suggest that newcomers may encounter a competitive housing market and a population skewed toward retirees and established professionals.

sections.heading: Housing Costs and Affordability
sections.text:
Homeownership is common in Scottsdale, with about 67% of occupied housing units owned rather than rented. The median value of owner‑occupied homes stands at $789,800, while the median gross rent is $2,013 per month. These figures place Scottsdale well above the national median, reflecting strong demand and limited supply.

Prospective residents should weigh the high median income of $110,886 against these costs. While the income level can support the market for many, those on tighter budgets may find the price points restrictive. Renters also face a premium, though the city’s rental market remains robust due to steady demand from workers in the tourism sector.

sections.heading: Geography, Boundaries and Climate
sections.text:
Scottsdale occupies 184.5 square miles in eastern Maricopa County, stretching 31 miles from north to south. It borders Phoenix to the west, the Tonto National Forest to the north, the McDowell Mountains to the east, and the Salt River to the south. The highest point, Butte Peak, reaches 4,890 ft.

The city sits in the Salt River Valley, also called the “Valley of the Sun,” within the Sonoran Desert. Its arid climate brings mild winters and extremely hot summers. Record temperatures range from a low of 16.0 °F on January 7, 1913, to a high of 122 °F on June 26, 1990. Residents enjoy abundant sunshine year‑round, but summer heat can be intense, influencing outdoor activities and energy use.

sections.heading: Economic Base and Major Employers
sections.text:
Tourism is the engine that powers Scottsdale’s economy, accounting for the majority of jobs and a sizable share of the city’s tax base. The city’s world‑renowned resorts, championship golf courses, upscale art galleries, and desert‑adventure attractions draw millions of visitors each year, sustaining a robust hospitality sector that includes hotels, restaurants, boutique shops, and entertainment venues. In 2023, the tourism industry alone supported roughly 30 % of the city’s employed workforce, making it the single largest employer in the metropolitan area.

The prosperity generated by this visitor‑driven economy is reflected in Scottsdale’s high median household income of $110,886, well above the national average. While the local economy has diversified over the past decade—adding health‑care providers, technology firms, and financial services—the city still feels the seasonal pulse of tourism. Summer heat can depress resort occupancy, while major events such as the Scottsdale Culinary Festival or the Waste Management Phoenix Open create temporary spikes in hiring for hospitality, retail, and event‑staff positions.

Despite these fluctuations, the job market remains resilient. The city’s 2020‑2024 ACS data shows a stable employment rate, with strong demand for skilled workers in hotel management, culinary arts, and retail merchandising. Moreover, the high home‑ownership rate (about 67 % of occupied units) and median home value of $789,800 indicate that many residents benefit from the steady income streams generated by tourism‑related businesses, reinforcing Scottsdale’s reputation as a financially vibrant place to live and work.

sections.heading: Lifestyle, Recreation and Community Feel
sections.text:
Scottsdale’s slogan, “The West’s Most Western Town,” captures its blend of modern amenities and desert heritage. Residents benefit from proximity to the McDowell Mountains and Tonto National Forest, offering hiking, biking and horseback riding. The city’s layout includes extensive park systems and a vibrant downtown with galleries, boutiques and dining.

The median age of 49 suggests a community oriented toward mature lifestyles, with many amenities catering to retirees and professionals. While the cost of living is high, the combination of high income, cultural offerings and outdoor recreation makes Scottsdale attractive for those who value a polished, active environment.

faq.a: The 2020 census recorded Scottsdale’s population at 241,361. The latest ACS 5‑year estimate (2020‑2024) places it at 243,821, showing modest growth since 2010.

faq.a: Scottsdale covers 184.5 square miles, stretching 31 miles north‑to‑south. It borders Phoenix on the west, Tonto National Forest to the north, the McDowell Mountains to the east, and the Salt River to the south.

faq.q: What is the climate like in Scottsdale, including record high and low temperatures?
faq.a: Scottsdale has an arid climate with mild winters and extremely hot summers. The record low is 16.0 °F (−8.9 °C) on January 7, 1913, and the record high is 122 °F (50 °C) on June 26, 1990.

faq.q: Which industry employs the most people in Scottsdale?
faq.a: Tourism is the city’s primary employer, supporting jobs in hotels, restaurants, retail and related services throughout Scottsdale.

conclusion: Scottsdale offers high income, strong tourism jobs and abundant outdoor recreation, but its housing costs and scorching summers may deter some. Weigh these factors against your budget and lifestyle to decide if Scottsdale, AZ is the right fit.

title: Blues schedule: Nashville, Detroit, Utah games in November 2026
summary: Check the St. Louis Blues schedule for Nov. 7 in Nashville, Nov. 10 vs Detroit, and the Utah road trip, plus lineups and injury updates.

The next home game is Tuesday, Nov. 10, against the Detroit Red Wings at 8 p.m. ET on TNT. After that, the club heads west to Utah for a Thursday road game. Below is a practical guide to the schedule, lineups, and injury news you need to know.

sections.heading: Nov. 7 Blues schedule in Nashville
sections.text: The Blues travel to Bridgestone Arena in Nashville on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. The puck drops at noon, giving fans a mid‑day showdown. Joel Hofer is projected to start in goal, while forward Mason McTavish will take warmups but remains a gametime decision. Coach has shifted Connor McMichael to center and Dalibor Dvorsky to wing for this matchup. These adjustments aim to boost offensive flow against the host team. The game offers a chance to see how the new line combinations perform before the upcoming home stretch.

sections.heading: Nov. 10 Blues schedule against Detroit Red Wings
sections.text: Back in St. Louis, the Blues host the Detroit Red Wings on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, at Enterprise Center. The broadcast begins at 8 p.m. ET on TNT. Entering the game, the Blues sit at 7‑8‑2 and are 13th in the Western Conference with 16 points. The injury report lists Torey Krug out for the season (ankle), Tyler Tucker out (knee), Adam Jecho out (personal), and Dillon Dubé out (neck). Despite these absences, the club hopes to capitalize on home‑ice advantage and climb the standings.

sections.heading: Upcoming road trip to Utah
sections.text: After the Detroit home game, the Blues continue their schedule with a road trip to Utah. The Thursday game following the Nov. 7 Nashville matchup will be against the Utah Mammoth. This marks the first away game after the Nashville visit. The travel schedule gives the team a chance to reset after two consecutive home games and test depth players in a different environment.

sections.heading: Potential return of Logan Mailloux
sections.text: Logan Mailloux could be cleared to rejoin the lineup either on Tuesday, Nov. 10, when the Blues host Detroit, or on Thursday during the Utah road game. The timing depends on the league’s clearance process and his health status. If he returns on Nov. 10, he would provide a boost to the forward group that is missing several key players due to injuries. Coaches will weigh his readiness against the team’s immediate needs.

Aleksanteri Kaskimaki is expected to stay in a top‑6 forward role on Thursday in New Jersey, according to the Nov. 7 lineup preview. title: Is Gilbert, AZ a Good Place to Live? Pros and Cons
summary: Discover the pros and cons of living in Gilbert, AZ with facts on population, income, housing, climate, and amenities.
intro: Gilbert, AZ ranks as a desirable suburb of Phoenix with a population of 287,285 in 2025, a median household income of $122,551, and a strong sense of community. Its hot arid climate, extensive open space, and proximity to the airport make it attractive, while high housing costs and rental rates are considerations. This guide breaks down the key advantages and drawbacks to help you decide if Gilbert is right for you.
bullets: Population over 280,000 with a young median age
Median household income exceeds $120k
Home values average $575,100; rent $2,110
Hot arid climate with mild winters
Over 600 acres of open space and 40+ sports fields

sections.heading: Population, Demographics, and Community Size
sections.text: Gilbert is the fourth‑most populous municipality in Arizona and the most populous incorporated town in the United States. The 2020‑2024 American Community Survey estimates a population of 280,262, while a 2025 count shows 287,285 residents. The median age is 36.1 years, indicating a relatively young community. About 73% of occupied housing units are owner‑occupied, reflecting stability and investment in the area. These figures suggest a growing, family‑friendly town with a solid base of homeowners.

sections.heading: Economic Outlook and Cost of Living
sections.text: Household earnings in Gilbert are strong, with a median income of $122,551 per year. This financial health supports local businesses and services. However, housing costs are notable. The median value of owner‑occupied homes stands at $575,100, and the median gross rent is $2,110 per month. Prospective residents should weigh these costs against the income levels and consider budgeting for higher housing expenses compared to many other regions.

sections.heading: Climate and Outdoor Recreation
sections.text:
Gilbert’s climate is classified as hot‑arid (Köppen BWh), meaning summers often soar above 100°F (38°C) while winters remain mild to warm, with average lows in the mid‑50s°F (12‑13°C). Although the heat can be intense, the low humidity makes outdoor pursuits more tolerable than in many other desert cities, and the pleasant winter months invite residents to enjoy the town’s extensive recreation network year‑round.  

Spanning 68.86 square miles—almost all of it land—Gilbert has devoted more than 600 acres to open‑space parks, nature trails, and natural preserves. These green corridors link over 40 well‑maintained sports fields, soccer complexes, baseball diamonds, and multi‑use courts, creating a seamless web for hikers, cyclists, and team‑sport enthusiasts. The town’s flagship spaces, such as the Heritage District Trail and the Gilbert Regional Park, offer paved paths shaded by native desert vegetation, while the Riparian Preserve provides bird‑watching and gentle walking routes that feel like a cool oasis after a hot day.  

Because the median age in Gilbert is just 36.1 years, the community skews active, and the high median household income of $122,551 supports a robust investment in amenities, from well‑lit trail lighting to modern fitness stations. Even with the summer heat, residents frequently schedule early‑morning runs, evening bike rides, or weekend pick‑up games, taking advantage of the town’s commitment to an active, outdoor‑oriented lifestyle. This blend of climate‑adapted design and abundant open space makes Gilbert a town where staying fit is both practical and enjoyable.

sections.heading: Location and Accessibility
sections.text:
Situated southeast of Phoenix, Gilbert enjoys a strategic position that blends suburban tranquility with easy access to the bustling metropolitan corridor of the Valley. Covering nearly 69 square miles of mostly flat desert terrain, the town sits directly south of Mesa, northeast of Chandler, and northwest of the rapidly growing community of Queen Creek. This placement places Gilbert at the crossroads of three major freeways—Loop 202 to the north, the I‑10 to the south, and the I‑285 (the “Santan Freeway”) skirting its eastern edge—allowing residents to reach downtown Phoenix, the airport, and surrounding employment hubs in roughly 30 minutes. Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, a key gateway for both business travelers and vacationers, is about a half‑hour’s drive away, making weekend getaways and long‑distance commutes remarkably convenient.

The town’s central location also supports a robust housing market: about 73 % of occupied units are owner‑occupied, with a median home value of $575,100, while renters face a median gross rent of $2,110 per month. With a 2025 population of 287,285—the fourth‑largest municipality in Arizona and the most populous incorporated town in the United States—Gilbert’s median age of 36.1 years reflects a youthful, family‑oriented community. High median household incomes of $122,551 further underscore the area’s economic vitality, enabling residents to take full advantage of the extensive network of open spaces, sports fields, and nearby cultural amenities while staying well‑connected to the greater Phoenix region.

sections.heading: Historical Roots and Community Identity
sections.text: Gilbert was incorporated on July 6, 1920, and its origins trace back to 1902 when William "Bobby" Gilbert provided land for the Arizona Eastern Railway. Early development included Ayer's Grocery Store in 1910, which also housed the first post office in 1912. The town grew with the settlement of Mormons fleeing Mexican colonies in 1912, forming the Gilbert Ward in 1918. These historical milestones shape a strong sense of identity and pride among residents.

faq.a: The town is about 30 minutes from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport, providing convenient access for travelers.
